introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá begins with a tree: grown from the seed of reality, fruitful for a time, then decayed, so that the seed must be sown again. The readings follow that figure through seasons, garments, clouds over the sun and yesterday’s food, and they speak sharply of leaders who have made religion a veil and of followers who hold what their fathers held. Much of the company agrees with them from inside older religions: the Hebrew prophets against empty worship, Jesus against the tradition of men, the Qur’an against following one’s fathers, the Dhammapada and Kabīr against outward marks, Milton and Dostoevsky against the shepherds. Others resist. Job says that a tree cut down will sprout again; Proverbs forbids moving the ancient landmark; Confucius calls himself a transmitter; Burke and Chesterton defend what is inherited; and the verses on which Christians and Muslims rest the finality of their faiths are set beside the readings that question it.
questions: The readings say that an old tree cannot become young again; Job says that at the scent of water it will bud. What evidence would count for either view of a religion, and what do the readings themselves offer as evidence?

Jeremiah calls his people back to “the old paths”, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of “turning back to the original foundation”, yet the readings also call for new teachings for a new age. How do return and newness fit together in them?

The prophets, Jesus and the Qur’an all blame religious leaders, and Jeremiah adds, “my people love to have it so”. Where do these readings place responsibility for the decay of a religion, and where would you?

Burke and Chesterton defend inherited belief as stored wisdom; the readings call it blind imitation, and Kant asks for the courage to use one’s own reason. What does a person owe to what he or she was taught?

“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever”; “This day have I perfected your religion for you.” How might someone who holds one of these verses dear hear the readings’ picture of seasons and daily food, and what in the readings is addressed to that person?

outside.why: The tree of religion “has fallen into a condition of decay”, and it is not reasonable to hold to it. Tennyson’s dying Arthur says as much of every good custom: the old order changes, lest one of them corrupt the world.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá would sow the seed again rather than keep a fruitless tree. In Jesus’ parable the dresser of the vineyard asks for one more year, to dig about the tree and dung it. How long is a barren tree to be given?
“Shall we say to the sun, ‘Go away! … you were here yesterday’?” The poet of Lamentations, in a ruined city, says that the mercies of the Lord are new every morning.

“When the season of spring appears … the whole world is rejuvenated.” The Song of Solomon has the lines by which that season has been announced ever since: the winter is past, the flowers appear on the earth.
“The True Gardener will again plant a tender sapling of the same stock.” Isaiah pictures renewal the same way: a rod out of the stem of Jesse, a branch from the old roots.
Forms and practices, says the reading, “are but garments” on the living limbs of truth. Kabīr has God say where He is not to be sought: not in temple or mosque, not in rites and ceremonies.
“A thirsty man will run after every fountain, he may drink bitter and stagnant water.” Jeremiah’s people do it by choice, leaving the fountain of living waters for cisterns they have hewn themselves.

The religionists are like students who “disputed with each other as to which master was the best”. Paul meets it within one church in its first years: I am of Paul, and I of Apollos. Is Christ divided?

“They have made the Law of God a cause and pretext for perversity and hatred.” Pascal, a believer, puts the observation in one sentence: men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as from religious conviction.

“The first duty and the basis of each religion is the love of God. Love has vanished.” The letter to Ephesus has the same charge against a church still busy and orthodox: thou hast left thy first love.

The imitations that crept in “were distinct from the teachings given by the prophets”. Jesus makes the distinction against the teachers of his day: ye lay aside the commandment of God and hold the tradition of men.
“It is the outward practices of religion that are so different … while the reality is always the same, and one.” Rūmī has the image for it: the lamps are different, but the Light is the same.

The student finds that the lives of the followers “do not ‘correspond’” with the teachings, and concludes against the teachers. Paul warns his own people of that inference: the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you.

The “law of correspondence” judges a religion by the conduct of its people. That is the Gospel’s own test for prophets: by their fruits ye shall know them. Does a tree’s bad season prove that the seed was false?
A people “accustomed to the expression of generosity in words only”. Ezekiel is told that his hearers come and listen as to a lovely song: they hear the words, but they do them not.

“Christ said if someone wrongs you, respond with kindness, yet now Christ’s followers are engaged in warfare … calling it a holy war.” The rebuke was first given to two disciples who wanted fire from heaven on a village.
Later generations “misconstrued their words” and “fabricated these false doctrines”. Jeremiah says it to those who boast that the law is with them: the pen of the scribes is in vain.

The reading lays the corruption of religion on priests who filled the people’s minds with dogmas. Jeremiah agrees about the priests and adds a clause: and my people love to have it so. What is the people’s share?
“The leaders of religions … have taken the Spirit captive.” Dostoevsky stages it: the Grand Inquisitor has Christ in his prison and tells him that he has come only to hinder the Church’s work.

“The way of God and the religion of God have ceased to be of any worth in the eyes of men.” Arnold heard the same thing on the English coast in those years: the long, withdrawing roar of the sea of faith.

People leave the churches dissatisfied, says the reading, “because they do not see spiritually”. Milton turns to the shepherds: blind mouths, and hungry sheep that look up and are not fed. Is the lack in the eyes of those who leave, or in what they were given?

“The material philosophers have overcome the religionists,” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, because religion is sunk in dogma. Bacon expected philosophy to end otherwise: a little inclines the mind to atheism, depth brings it about to religion. Which has the last three centuries borne out?

A government turns against religion altogether, and the reading blames “the mistakes made by the leaders of religion”. Marx’s famous sentence finds the cause deeper: religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, and will go when the oppression goes. Is the fault in the leaders or in the thing?

“Two basic pillars: willing submission of one’s own will to the divine Will, and uprightness”, against “empty formalism”. Micah’s summary has the same shape: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with thy God.
“Many ages roll by and the spirit of these words are forgotten.” The book of Judges needs only one generation: another arose that knew not the Lord, nor the works he had done.

“We must relinquish all the rituals and forms which have accumulated … completely hiding It from our views.” Tagore says it to a worshipper in a shut temple: leave this chanting; open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee.
“There is need of turning back to the original foundation.” Renewal here is a return, and Jeremiah’s call is the same: ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein.

“The first teaching is that man should investigate reality”, against “imitations of ancestral forms of belief”. Kant’s essay of 1784 gave the age its motto for the same step: have courage to use your own reason.

All souls “should consider it incumbent upon them to investigate reality”. The Qur’an gives the duty and its reason: follow not that of which thou hast no knowledge; hearing, sight and heart will each be asked.

The reading calls inherited belief “blind imitations”, productive of strife. Burke defends it: the private stock of reason in each man is small, and prejudice carries the wisdom of ages. What would each of them say a person owes to what he was taught?
“The nations had, like tattered garments long outworn, fallen into a pitiful condition.” The Gītā uses the figure of the soul and its bodies: worn-out robes are laid aside and new ones taken.

“From the continual imitation of ancient and worn-out ways, the world had grown dark.” Emerson opens his first book with the same complaint and the same demand: why should not we also enjoy an original relation to the universe?

“The people … must be set completely free from their old patterns of thought.” Chesterton calls tradition the democracy of the dead, and refuses to be ruled only by those who happen to be walking about. What is lost when a people is set free of its dead?

“New thinking is needed and new teachings are necessary that are the spirit of this age.” Lowell’s lines, written against slavery, became a hymn: new occasions teach new duties; time makes ancient good uncouth.

The reading calls this “a luminous age” that requires “a new illumination”. The Preacher has seen ages come and go: is there anything of which it may be said, See, this is new? How would he be answered?
“Do you see today anything remaining among the people of that original foundation?” The church at Sardis is told the same in one line: thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.

“Look at Islam—they are entirely heedless of the divine counsels and admonitions in the Quran.” The Qur’an records the complaint beforehand, in the mouth of its own messenger: my folk make this Qur’an of no account.
“The reins of every community have fallen into the grasp of foolish leaders, who lead after their own whims.” The saying about the blind leading the blind was spoken of religious teachers.
This is the prophecy the reading interprets: the “sun” and “moon” that are darkened are the teachings and laws of the earlier Dispensation, which “cease to exert their influence”.
“On their tongue the mention of God hath become an empty name.” Isaiah hears the same worship: near with the mouth, the heart far off, and a fear of God that is taught by the precept of men.

“Every follower of a religion is born into that religion with what it containeth, without insight or understanding.” The Qur’an gives the answer such followers make: we follow that wherein we found our fathers.
“Most people still know not what Day this is.” Jesus says it of people who can read tomorrow’s weather in the evening sky and cannot discern the signs of the times.

“They worship the idols of vain imaginings.” Bacon, cataloguing the idols of the mind, names the mechanism: the understanding is no dry light, and what a man had rather were true he more readily believes.
“We must free ourselves from these intolerable burdens.” The burdens are in the Gospel too, bound on men’s shoulders by teachers who will not move them with one of their fingers.

The reading would “discard these fantastic traditions which have been handed to us as … precious heirlooms from ancestors”. Proverbs forbids exactly that: remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set. How is a landmark told from a burden?
“The primary cause and reason for the veiling of mankind have been … the divines.” Jesus says it to the lawyers: ye have taken away the key of knowledge, and hindered those who were entering.
“The dust of ignorance, like a disease of the eyes, has prevented them from beholding.” In John the disease is thinking oneself well: now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.

The religions “implore and supplicate … for the meeting”, and when the Sun shone “all remained occupied with their own idle fancies”. Jesus weeps over a praying city that did not know the time of its visitation.
“All the people of the world were waiting and still wait, yet … all turned away.” John’s prologue says it in a line: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.

For twelve hundred years the divines “beseeched and supplicated for the days of His manifestation”, then denied. Jesus describes the same piety: building the tombs of the prophets and being sure one would not have killed them.

The reading charges that the people of the Bayán “opposed Us without any clear proof”. Gamaliel’s counsel to a council sure of its ground is what such opponents might have been asked for: leave them alone; if it be of God ye cannot overthrow it.

“The weapon of war and shield of the idolaters is the mention of death and detachment from the world”: pious words used as arms. Antonio’s remark is the proverb for it: the devil can cite Scripture for his purpose.
“Should colocynth claim to be sugar, those with taste will not accept it.” The First Epistle of John lays the same duty on believers: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits.

Some are kept from the shore “by ancient allusions to the worn-out and obsolete notion of succession”. John the Baptist dismisses an older claim by descent: think not to say, We have Abraham to our father.

The reading calls succession a “worn-out and obsolete notion”. The Mishnah’s Sayings of the Fathers opens on a succession, Moses to Joshua to the elders to the prophets, as the way a revelation is kept at all. When does a chain of hands preserve, and when does it replace?
“Observe for yourself whether it is truth or spoken from desire.” Paul’s rule for the churches is as short: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
The people of the Bayán “deny that which the people of the Furqan have acknowledged”. Jesus argues in the same form with those who trust in Moses: had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me.
“They … perverted the words of God from their places.” The phrase is the Qur’an’s, said of an earlier people of a Book: they change words from their context and forget a part of what they were told.

Nothing shall profit, “nor any name among all names, nor that which ye have clung to of tales and traditions”. Jeremiah stands at the gate with the same warning against a holy formula repeated three times.

“The tastes of men have changed … The contrary winds of the world, and its colors, have provoked a cold.” Wordsworth diagnoses the same dullness: the world is too much with us, and we are out of tune.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says of Buddhists that “many worship idols although their teaching forbids it”. The teaching he may have in mind is the Buddha’s last: be lamps unto yourselves; look not for refuge to anyone besides.

“The Buddhists have entirely deviated from the path of Buddha.” The Dhammapada already knows the religion of outward marks, and says what the hair and the goat-skins are worth when within there is ravening.

In the reading a ruler finds his religion out of date and looks among the others for a replacement. Vivekananda told the Parliament of Religions the opposite: no one is to become another, but each to grow by his own law. Can an old religion be renewed from within?

The reading wants minds in China unshackled “from the rusty chains of ancestral traditions”. Confucius, the chief of those ancestors, described himself as a transmitter and not a maker, believing in and loving the ancients. Is that love the chain, or what the chain was forged from?

Against “ancestral traditions” the reading sets new teachers. Confucius has a third possibility: one who keeps cherishing his old knowledge so as continually to be acquiring new. What would such a teacher look like in the reading’s terms?
“When the Greeks and Romans became Christians, some of the idolatrous customs were incorporated into Christianity.” Tertullian fought that mixture at the time: what has Athens to do with Jerusalem?
Customs brought in “only as symbols” were afterwards “interpreted literally”. The letter to the Colossians treats holy days and observances as a shadow of things to come, not the body.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá recalls that John’s baptism “served to awaken and admonish the people and to cause them to repent”. John says so himself, and points past the water to a baptism with the Holy Ghost and with fire.

A garden tended for a hundred years, “if it be neglected for a single year … will become a wilderness”. Isaiah’s vineyard, planted with the choicest vine, brought forth wild grapes: he looked for judgment, but behold oppression.
“Of the law of God naught remains but a name, and of the divine teachings naught but an outward form.” The Second Letter to Timothy has the phrase: a form of godliness, denying the power thereof.

“As nature needs a springtime to revive the trees, so the spiritual nature needs a springtime.” The promise after the flood is the natural half of the likeness: seedtime and harvest, summer and winter shall not cease.

The reading gives the dispensation of Moses its spring, summer, autumn and winter. The Preacher’s catalogue of times begins with the same two: a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted.

“Then the spiritual spring spreads its tent once more.” The psalmist sees the same turn in nature: the breath is taken away and they die; the spirit is sent forth, and the face of the earth is renewed.
“All the created phenomena are subject to the law of change.” The psalm says it of the heavens themselves, which wax old like a garment and are changed, while One remains the same.

Some believe that the very old trees “will again become young … This is impossible.” Job says the contrary of a tree: though the root wax old and the stock die, at the scent of water it will bud. Which is truer of a religion, and how would one know?
Religion, once a comely youth, “is stricken with old age”. The Epistle to the Hebrews speaks so of the first covenant: that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.

“A tree which hath been in existence for two thousand years or more will never bring new and fresh fruits.” The same epistle holds the conviction this meets in a Christian hearer: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Are the two speaking of the same thing?
“Every new day requires new food, you cannot partake of the decayed food of yesterday.” The manna in the wilderness taught it literally: kept till morning, it bred worms.

The reading asks, as an absurdity, whether “the Heavenly Table is ended” and no Manifestation will appear. This is the verse on which most Muslims rest the belief that prophecy is closed. How does the reading’s figure of daily food bear on it?
Against the idea that revelation has ended, the Gospel has Jesus leave his own teaching open: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
When “the divine dispensary is closed … people express joy”. Jesus uses the physician’s figure of those who feel no need of him: they that be whole need not a physician.

“Religion must undergo change; for religion is a manifested thing in the world.” Burke, no friend of innovation, says the same of a state: without the means of some change it is without the means of its conservation.

The reading divides: change belongs to created things, “constancy or unchangeableness” to the essence. Malachi speaks for the essence: I am the Lord, I change not. Where does religion fall between the two, as the reading draws the line?
“Christ gave new life and effect to the meanings of the ancient law.” This is how he describes his own work in the Sermon on the Mount: not to destroy, but to fulfil.
“God sent His prophets to shine upon them with the Spring of the Sun of righteousness.” The phrase is Malachi’s, the last word of the prophets before a long silence.
“It was very long since the coming of a Prophet, and they needed a new one.” Krishna gives the rule in the Gītā: when righteousness declines, I rise, from age to age.

“Every divine religious law was complete for its time. The renewal of the laws of God … in each cycle are necessary.” The Qur’an speaks of its own verses in that way: none is abrogated but a better or the like is brought.

Secondary teachings “were perfectly suited to their own time”, and their changing serves “the security and prosperity of all humankind”. Jesus gives the principle for one law: the sabbath was made for man.
“The laws of the previous age do not suffice for this great century.” New wine, says Jesus, is not put into old bottles; it needs new ones, and both are preserved.

“The spiritual laws … must be renewed and divine matters must be made new.” Jude writes to defend a faith “once delivered unto the saints”. What in a religion is delivered once, and what, on the reading’s account, must be delivered again?
“As everything evolves, so also does religion—as witness the doctrines that are losing their influence today.” Tennyson: our little systems have their day; they are but broken lights of thee.
“Nor attach ourselves to any form or ritual which is in opposition to moral evolution.” Hosea states the priority as God’s own: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.

“We must get rid of all glosses, Talmuds, codes of divinity, and clerical law.” Jesus’ complaint is narrower: the tithe of mint is paid and the weightier matters of the law are left undone, though the lesser ought not to be left either.

The reported words hold that revelations “were for their own day and environment”. The Qur’an says of itself, This day have I perfected your religion for you. How does a believer in that verse hear the claim that its application belongs to its century?
“If the religion of Moses had not changed, Christ would not have appeared.” Jeremiah, within the religion of Moses, promises a new covenant, not according to the one made with the fathers.
“Not until night falls will a new day dawn.” Jesus gives the law of it from the field: unless a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abides alone.
“The true dawn broke and divine lights shone forth, and all these virtues were renewed on this day.” The seer of Patmos hears it from the throne: Behold, I make all things new.

The reading expects people to study the existing religions “to see which religion conforms to the exigencies of the time”. Gandhi thought the need of the moment was not one religion but mutual respect among many. What would each make of the other’s hope?
Bahá’u’lláh summons kings and subjects so “that lost honour be restored”. The book of Lamentations ends on that prayer: turn thou us unto thee, and renew our days as of old.

“With what power and ascendancy did the people of unity appear in the first days, and into what abasement … are they now fallen!” The Preacher distrusts the question: say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? When is it wise to ask it?

quran-write-with-their-hands.text: Therefore woe be unto those who write the Scripture with their hands and then say, "This is from Allah," that they may purchase a small gain therewith. Woe unto them for that their hands have written, and woe unto them for that they earn thereby.

quran-split-into-sects.text: Of those who split up their religion and became schismatics, each sect exulting in its tenets.

quran-change-what-is-in-their-hearts.text: For him are angels ranged before him and behind him, who guard him by Allah's command. Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts; and if Allah willeth misfortune for a folk there is none that can repel it, nor have they a defender beside Him.

quran-of-no-account.text: And the messenger saith: O my Lord! Lo! mine own folk make this Qur'an of no account.

quran-every-nation-its-term.text: And every nation hath its term, and when its term cometh, they cannot put it off an hour nor yet advance (it).

quran-follow-not-without-knowledge.text: (O man), follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge. Lo! the hearing and the sight and the heart - of each of these it will be asked.

quran-be-not-as-those-who-separated.text: And be ye not as those who separated and disputed after the clear proofs had come unto them. For such there is an awful doom,

quran-change-words-from-context.text: And because of their breaking their covenant, We have cursed them and made hard their hearts. They change words from their context and forget a part of that whereof they were admonished. Thou wilt not cease to discover treachery from all save a few of them. But bear with them and pardon them. Lo! Allah loveth the kindly.

quran-monasticism-invented.text: Then We caused Our messengers to follow in their footsteps; and We caused Jesus, son of Mary, to follow, and gave him the Gospel, and placed compassion and mercy in the hearts of those who followed him. But monasticism they invented - We ordained it not for them - only seeking Allah's pleasure, and they observed it not with right observance. So We give those of them who believe their reward, but many of them are evil-livers.

emerson-sepulchres-of-the-fathers.text: Our age is retrospective. It builds the sepulchres of the fathers. It writes biographies, histories, and criticism. The foregoing generations beheld God and nature face to face; we, through their eyes. Why should not we also enjoy an original relation to the universe?
emerson-sepulchres-of-the-fathers.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

kant-sapere-aude.text: Enlightenment is man's release from his self-incurred tutelage. Tutelage is man's inability to make use of his understanding without direction from another. … Sapere aude! "Have courage to use your own reason!" - that is the motto of enlightenment
kant-sapere-aude.author: Immanuel Kant
kant-sapere-aude.work: An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?

analects-transmitter-not-maker.text: A transmitter and not a maker, believing in and loving the ancients, I venture to compare myself with our old P'ang
analects-transmitter-not-maker.author: Confucius

analects-old-knowledge-new.text: If a man keeps cherishing his old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new, he may be a teacher of others
analects-old-knowledge-new.author: Confucius

analects-rites-without-virtue.text: If a man be without the virtues proper to humanity, what has he to do with the rites of propriety? If a man be without the virtues proper to humanity, what has he to do with music?
analects-rites-without-virtue.author: Confucius

dhammapada-platted-hair.text: A man does not become a Brahmana by his platted hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana. What is the use of platted hair, O fool! what of the raiment of goat-skins? Within thee there is ravening, but the outside thou makest clean

rumi-inside-and-state-of-heart.text: I regard not the outside and the words, / I regard the inside and the state of heart. / I look at the heart if it be humble, / Though the words may be the reverse of humble
rumi-inside-and-state-of-heart.author: Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī
rumi-inside-and-state-of-heart.locator: Book II, Moses and the shepherd

milton-hungry-sheep.text: Blind mouthes! that scarce themselves know how to hold / A Sheep-hook, or have learn'd ought els the least / That to the faithfull Herdmans art belongs! / What recks it them? What need they? They are sped; / And when they list, their lean and flashy songs / Grate on their scrannel Pipes of wretched straw, / The hungry Sheep look up, and are not fed, / But swoln with wind, and the rank mist they draw, / Rot inwardly and foul contagian spread
milton-hungry-sheep.author: John Milton

blake-garden-of-love.text: And the gates of this chapel were shut, / And Thou shalt not writ over the door; / So I turn'd to the Garden of Love, / That so many sweet flowers bore. / And I saw it was filled with graves, / And tomb-stones where flowers should be: / And Priests in black gowns, were walking their rounds, / And binding with briars my joys & desires
blake-garden-of-love.author: William Blake

tennyson-honest-doubt.text: Perplext in faith, but pure in deeds, / At last he beat his music out. / There lives more faith in honest doubt, / Believe me, than in half the creeds
tennyson-honest-doubt.author: Alfred Tennyson

kabir-neither-temple-nor-mosque.text: O servant, where dost thou seek Me? Lo! I am beside thee. I am neither in temple nor in mosque: I am neither in Kaaba nor in Kailash: Neither am I in rites and ceremonies, nor in Yoga and renunciation. If thou art a true seeker, thou shalt at once see Me: thou shalt meet Me in a moment of time. Kabir says, "O Sadhu! God is the breath of all breath
kabir-neither-temple-nor-mosque.author: Kabīr

chesterton-democracy-of-the-dead.text: Tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors. It is the democracy of the dead. Tradition refuses to submit to the small and arrogant oligarchy of those who merely happen to be walking about
chesterton-democracy-of-the-dead.author: G. K. Chesterton

burke-means-of-change.text: A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation. Without such means it might even risk the loss of that part of the constitution which it wished the most religiously to preserve
burke-means-of-change.author: Edmund Burke
burke-means-of-change.work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
